\gap\ tatkathanamathādhikyata iti prakaraṇasambandhaḥ| liṅgaṃ parameśvarapūjādhikaraṇam| amarārcitam iti liṅgārādhanatastatprāptirjanānāmiti jñāpayitum| tathā coktaṃ śrīmanmaye---
children.translated_text: [Gap] The discussion of that is now from the section on superiority — such is the section-connection. The <s>liṅga</s> is the locus of worship of <s>Parameśvara</s>. 'Worshipped by the immortals' — to indicate that by worshipping the <s>liṅga</s>, people attain Him. As stated in the blessed <s>Maya</s> [tantra]:

children.text:
ādityā vasavo rudrā ṛṣayaśca mahaujasaḥ|
vidhivalliṅgamārādhya padamisṭ.atamaṃ gatāḥ|| iti|
children.translated_text: 'The <s>Ādityas</s>, <s>Vasus</s>, <s>Rudras</s>, and sages of great splendor — having worshipped the <s>liṅga</s> according to rule, they attained the most desired station.'
Manifest

children.text: pratimā| avyaktam anabhivyaktāṅgam| ubhayātmakaṃ vyaktāvyaktaṃ mukhaliṅgamityarthaḥ| \gap\ siddhyarthaṃ sādhaka ātmanaḥ kṛte sthāpayet paraiḥ samayisādhakaputrakādibhiḥ abhyarthito vā guruḥ ācāryaḥ pratiṣṭhāpayet| parairiti viśeṣaṇād guroḥ pare ye sādhakādayastaistadevaṃsiddhaye ātmanaḥ pratiṣṭhā kāryā| ācāryeṇa tu caturṇāmapīti tātparyam||
children.translated_text: means an image. 'Unmanifest' means having unexpressed limbs. 'Of both natures' means manifest-and-unmanifest — meaning a <s>mukha-liṅga</s> (liṅga with faces). [Gap] For the purpose of attainment, the <s>sādhaka</s> should install [a <s>liṅga</s>] for himself; or the teacher (<s>guru</s>, <s>ācārya</s>), being requested by others — <s>samayīs</s>, <s>sādhakas</s>, <s>putrakas</s>, and the like — should install [it]. By the qualifier 'by others,' those other than the teacher — <s>sādhakas</s> and the rest — should have the installation done for their own attainment. But by the <s>ācārya</s>, for all four — this is the purport.
He specifies that very <s>liṅga</s>:
That [<s>liṅga</s>] may be made of stone, metal, clay, jewel,
or wood — established on the ground;
as far as [it is] ordained by the Omniscient One —
for one desiring enjoyments, or for another.
[Vṛtti:]

children.text: tad liṅgaṃ bubhukṣoḥ bhogecchoḥ [itarasya vā] anyasya vā munerarcane prabhavatīti| yataḥ sarvajñatvamato 'khilakartṛprasaram| tathā bāhulyena śailalohamṛdratnadāruprakṛtijaṃ praśastam| kvaccittu svaśāstrāmnātānyaprakṛtijamapi bhāvyam||
children.translated_text: That <s>liṅga</s> is efficacious for the worship of one desiring enjoyments, [or for another] or another — a sage. Because of His omniscience, [His] agency extends to all. Also, predominantly, [a <s>liṅga</s>] made of stone, metal, clay, jewel, or wood is praiseworthy. But in some cases, [a <s>liṅga</s>] born of other materials taught in one's own scripture should also be contemplated.
By priority of the first — the jewel-made — he states the measurement:
One finger [in height] up to two hands (24 fingers)
for a jewel-made [<s>liṅga</s>] — not more than that.
[Vṛtti:]
One finger

children.translated_text: Now, having considered the state of self-mastery
[or] one's own difficult-to-accomplish jurisdiction,
the preceptor and others, desiring to conquer,
should strive for self-mastery.
That self-mastery — yogic [attainment] —
is accomplished by one who has conquered the senses.
From the practice of <s>prāṇāyāma</s> and the rest,
[comes] mastery over the senses, gradually.
<s>Prāṇāyāma</s> (breath-control), <s>pratyāhāra</s> (sense-withdrawal),
<s>dhāraṇā</s> (concentration), <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation), <s>vīkṣaṇa</s> (contemplation),
<s>japa</s> (recitation), <s>samādhi</s> (absorption) — these are the limbs;
yoga itself is the eighth, the principal [member].
<s>Prāṇa</s> (breath) is the wind previously described;
<s>āyāma</s> is its exertion —
characterized by expulsion (<s>preraṇa</s>), retention (<s>ākṛṣṭi</s>), and suspension (<s>saṃrodha</s>) —
which removes the defects of ritual acts.
Then, when there is a taste of [subtle] pleasure
for the mind that has [thus] functioned through those [breaths],
<s>pratyāhāra</s> (sense-withdrawal) should be practiced —
the complete turning back [of the senses] from all [objects].
Through that, when the contact between senses and objects
has ceased, the mind, accumulated [in concentration],
becomes fit for <s>dhāraṇā</s> (concentration)
upon a locus chosen at will.
Thought directed toward that [object] is <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation);
and that [meditation], as instructed, repeated again and again,
reaches single-pointed continuity —
that is ordained as <s>samādhi</s> (absorption).
<s>Japa</s> (recitation) is the utterance of that [mantra] —
the bringing face-to-face of the object of meditation, O sage.
<s>Ūha</s> (<s>abhivīkṣaṇa</s>, contemplation) is the object —
the [investigation] that arises immediately after conceptual thought.
When one knows the station to be abandoned
and that to be adopted, and what sustains that [station],
and the adversary [of the favorable],
and what further sustains that [adversary] —
for the yogin who has exerted himself
in these [limbs] separately and combined,
powers shine forth, pervading the universe,
like the rays of the sun.
No man can control him —
neither <s>Rākṣasas</s>, <s>Dānavas</s>, nor humans.
Shining beyond these,
with the radiance of [supernatural] sight, action, and vital force —
the cause of the mind's withdrawal
is the exertion of the breath through contact [with practice].
The withdrawal [of breath] is the root of <s>dhāraṇā</s> and the rest;
[and <s>dhāraṇā</s>] is the root of everything — thus, from that [breath-control, all follows].
'O best of gods, [please explain] in detail
that which is far removed [from common knowledge],
and whatever other means there may be
for yogic attainment — let it be told.'
'It cannot be spoken of at length
out of fear of digression from the [present] topic.
But since the question must necessarily be answered,
a summary is stated [nevertheless]:'
Having discharged urine and the like according to rule,
with one, half, ten, and seven
clods of earth — the genitals, anus, left [hand],
and pair of hands should be purified.
The vow-holder, having sipped water twice, thrice,
having wiped the face twice, should touch
his own arms, navel, and heart —
twice or thrice, purified below.
Healthy, having eaten what is beneficial and digested,
in a house enclosed by three walls,
or in a forest and the like, free from disturbance —
seated on his own seat, facing north.
Having bowed to <s>Maheśāna</s> (the Great Lord),
<s>Umā</s>, <s>Skanda</s>, and <s>Gaṇādhipa</s> (Gaṇeśa),
with neck, head, and chest held straight,
with both eyes fixed on the tip of the nose,
protecting the testicles with both heels,
teeth not touching teeth,
body held firm, placing the tongue
at the tip of the teeth, well-settled,
one should expel the breath (<s>māruta</s>) to the limit of one's capacity
through one nostril;
that is <s>recaka</s> (exhalation); through its practice,
in the activities of piercing (<s>vedha</s>) and scattering (<s>vikṣipta</s>),
one gradually attains the capacity
even in extended objects;
filling the body to the limit of [its] capacity
with external air —
that is <s>pūraka</s> (inhalation); through its practice,
one can draw in even what is very heavy;
abandoning both expulsion and retention —
that restraint is known as <s>kumbhaka</s> (retention).
Through its practice, the power of restraint
becomes manifest, unobstructed;
for one thus practicing, the wise [yogin],
in the paths of <s>Soma</s> (moon), <s>Sūrya</s> (sun), and <s>Īśa</s> (lord),
having understood the fitness for the properties of those [paths],
the <s>yogin</s> should accomplish what is desired:
<s>pūraka</s> or <s>kumbhaka</s>
should be practiced when the lunar path is active,
for the purpose of nourishment, conquest of death, and the like,
for oneself or another; <s>recaka</s>
for igniting fire without [an actual] fire, for drying up
a tree, for destroying a seed,
for stunning, maddening, blazing up poison,
and other such [hostile acts] — <s>recaka</s> [is used];
in meditation, worship, <s>japa</s>, and the like,
and in the abandonment of the body in <s>Śaṅkara</s>'s [path] —
<s>kumbhaka</s> and <s>recaka</s> are prescribed;
and in initiation (<s>dīkṣā</s>) and installation [rites].
The junior, middle, and senior [types of prāṇāyāma]
are [measured] by <s>tālas</s> (beats) of twelve and upward.
A <s>tāla</s> [is measured by] twelve revolutions
around the circumference of the knee;
that [prāṇāyāma] which is accompanied by meditation and <s>japa</s>
is <s>sagarbha</s> (with seed); the other, without that, [is <s>agarbha</s>].
As the <s>sagarbha</s> [serves] for the stability
of the mind, the other does not [do so];
the <s>agarbha</s> too destroys the sin committed at night
[when practiced] in the morning, and the sin committed by day [when practiced] at the end of the day;
the wavering of the senses (<s>deva</s>) that are rushing about;
[the practitioner] becomes bathed in sacred waters,
initiated in all sacrifices,
a vessel for the ancestors — he who constantly
practices this <s>sagarbha</s> [prāṇāyāma];
one should meditate on the deity (<s>deva</s>) who has gone beyond the paths,
and always recite his name-<s>mantra</s>.
Now, the <s>tattvas</s> beginning with earth,
or those presiding over their forms —
since an unconscious <s>tattva</s>,
even when accomplished, is not a helper —
one should meditate on the body of <s>Śiva</s>; therefore,
whatever is desired,
for the accomplishment of <s>dhāraṇās</s> (concentrations) and the like,
and of the functions of breath,
the wise one should perform <s>sagarbha kumbhaka</s>
with undivided mind,
[for] the time of twelve <s>arkas</s> (sun-measures);
having established mental stability,
one attains the designation of <s>dhāraṇā</s> (concentration),
because of the granting of the accomplishment of <s>dhāraṇā</s>.
The word <s>dhāraṇā</s> means 'stability';
also 'place,' by metaphorical usage.
The places of the beginner are these —
<s>yavanyā</s> (barley-shaped) and the like — not otherwise;
those are golden, snow-white, luminous,
dark, and transparent in appearance,
having the shapes of an altar-half, a crescent, a triangle,
a circle, and a lotus,
[serving] for the attainment of stability, nourishment, burning,
impelling, and emptiness.
They are accompanied by <s>vajra</s> (thunderbolt), lotus, flame,
<s>bindu</s> (point), and <s>śūnya</s> (void);
hostile, favorable,
or neutral — having understood [which],
the <s>yogin</s> should employ them singly or combined
for the accomplishment of what is desired.
In what place should the form of <s>dhāraṇā</s>
be contemplated by the wise one?
And what is the fruit of [employing them]
singly or combined — tell [us], O Lord of the gods!
In the heart, when the mind is agitated,
the knower of purposes should concentrate on earth;
water in the throat when thirsty;
fire in the belly when the digestive fire is weak;
for the accomplishment of the functions of <s>prāṇa</s> and the like,
wind in the heart, throat, and the like;
space for overcoming poison and the like —
wherever there is use for them.
Space [is friendly] in all elements;
water, wind, fire, and earth;
water and fire; earth and wind;
water and earth; fire and wind —
[these are] neutral, hostile, and friendly
in groups of four, pair by pair.
Having understood this, the wise one
should apply them for the accomplishment of what is desired.
What are the places of the <s>prāṇa</s> and other
functions in this body?
And when those are conquered, what results?
Tell [us], O best of the gods!
Through concentration on the heart, navel, chest, throat,
and back regions —
the <s>yogin</s> attains conquest
of the functions of <s>praṇayana</s> (exhalation) and the rest.
Having conquered <s>praṇayana</s>, one holds
the body of the self at will;
having conquered <s>apanayana</s> (downward breath), one eats
and does not release feces and the like;
having conquered <s>unnayana</s> (upward breath), one attains
mastery over speech and other qualities;
from the conquest of the <s>samāna</s> function,
one becomes free from aging, self-controlled;
mastery over bodily movements
results from conquering <s>vinamana</s> (bowing/distributing breath);
non-contact with mud, water, and thorns,
marvelous inexhaustible vigor.
Twelve <s>dhāraṇās</s> constitute <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation),
which produces the arising of divine vision;
<s>samādhi</s> — twelve [<s>dhyānas</s>] — is the cause
of <s>aṇimā</s> (becoming minute) and the other [siddhis];
even without <s>prāṇāyāma</s>, one who thus
has a controlled self, established in mind,
practicing, attains
the immediately following stated qualities;
whatever object, as instructed,
is attained through the sequential yoga [of dhāraṇā, dhyāna, samādhi],
in each of those, one's consciousness-manifestation
becomes of the scope of pervading that [object].
Thus, when established in the external [objects], having surveyed
everything with one's own eye,
abandoning all objects,
one should practice the <s>Śiva-tattva</s>;
abiding in <s>prāṇāyāma</s> and the like
that contain <s>Śiva</s> as their seed —
the being who relinquishes the breaths
attains <s>Śiva</s>-nature;
the supreme form of <s>Maheśa</s>
can never be meditated upon [as an object],
because of [its] variety, it is imagined through error;
how then can there be fixation of the mind on that?
Even in the earthly [<s>dhāraṇā</s>] with varied marks,
[it is] not the [true] object of meditation or concentration; yet then,
even so, <s>yogins</s> are heard to have attained accomplishment
through practice of those two [dhāraṇā and dhyāna].
How can there be mental stability
for one whose mind is overwhelmed by sense-enjoyments?
<s>Hara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) did not teach this practice
with reference to souls (<s>aṇu</s>) that are not detached;
even the entire world can be brought
under mastery, gradually,
let alone the wondrous body, by those who are self-controlled,
rich in the practice of detachment.
And what is this limitation of form
for the one conjoined with all-pervading superintendence,
who at all times, for all beings,
is a helper in all ways?
Having imagined with one's own mind
the places, forms, and measures [for meditation],
wherever the mind comes to rest,
that should be meditated upon again and again;
thereby, stability of the mind
[and] qualities with special [powers], gradually,
unfolding the <s>yoga</s>-impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>),
arise for the one whose obstacles are destroyed;
thus, for one who practices correctly,
even without the imagining of forms,
for this one who contemplates nothing,
one's own true form unfolds —
of the nature of all-seeing, all-acting,
blissful, imperishable [..];
having attained which, one does not again
enter the conjunction of suffering, the bearer of inauspiciousness;
this is the secret of all secrets,
praised by <s>Siddhas</s> and immortals;
the direct vision of <s>Śambhu</s>,
the supreme purifier;
this should not be given to one who has dwelt [in study] for but a short time,
nor to one who is excessively negligent,
nor to one who lacks intelligence, nor to one without austerity,
nor to one who does not worship <s>Śiva</s>.
Through the practice of this, illuminated by the rays of divine accomplishments,
having sported in desired worlds,
in due time, having abandoned the body that is with-outflow, one abides
in one's own Self alone, dwelling in wondrous activity.
